The acidic solution was added to the reactor with a volume of 25 mL. The leaching conditions including acid species, acid concentration, reductant content and pH of the leaching solution were examined. Samples were taken out at leaching time of t (t ≤5 min) and identified by ICP-OES (ICP-OES, iCAP 6300, Radial, Thermo Scientific) to find the local leaching parameters for leaching speeds. After leaching, the residues (undissolved organic binder and conductive reagent) and Al foil were vacuum filtered immediately. The leachate was analyzed by ICP-OES to get the local leaching parameters of metals for recovery rate.           "text": "## 3.1. Understanding the importance of different leaching parameters\nTo understand the importance of different parameters, the leaching parameters for LiCoO2 leaching processes were summarized in Table S2. The influence level was defined as a variable to evaluate the importance of different leaching parameters. A higher influence level means the parameter is more important for the leaching process and vice versa. The influence levels of the leaching parameters can be found in the supplementary materials, and the order from high to low is as follows: the acid species and concentration, leaching time, reductant species and concentration, S/L ratio, reaction temperature, stirring speed (Fig. S2).\nThe summary of the chemical properties of different acids were concluded in Table S3. To clearly explain the results in the following figures, the acids were numbered by serial number from A to L (Table S3). The existing acids in the leaching processes of LiCoO for spent LIBs are divided into inorganic acids (acid A to C) and organic acids (acid D to L). Among the mineral acids, sulfuric acid (acid B) is frequently used for the recycling of spent LIBs. For organic acids, citric acid (acid E) is the most frequently used organic acid.\nBased on Table S2 where the leaching results are similar (Li > 95% and Co > 90%), the relationship between S/L ratio and the concentration of acid is presented in Fig. 1. The black points represent the concentrations and the corresponding S / L ratios, while the regions of the different colors are the range covered by the black points of the corresponding acid leaching process. It can be confirmed from Fig. 1 that the leaching processes of inorganic acids are mostly concentrated at 3–6 mol/L with S/L ratios higher than 50 g/L (mostly 100 g/L). For organic acid leaching process, acid concentrations are generally only 1–2 mol/L, the treatments of cathode scrap are carried out with S / L ratio lower than 50 g/L, and the cathode material treatment capacity of unit volume of organic acid solution is much less than that of the inorganic acid solution. The distinction of the organic and inorganic acids is mainly because of the different pKa values, the organic acids have higher pKa values which make the ionization of hydrogen ion more difficult than inorganic acids. Therefore, the organic acid can be considered as a kind of buffering solution which can also realize the leaching efficiency but the treatment capacity is lower than inorganic acid because of the ionization balance of H+.\nFrom the perspective of industry, the inorganic acids act as leaching acid with the concentration of 1.5 mol/L–3 mol/L while the S/L ratios are from 100 g/L to 200 g/L (Yu et al., 2016). As shown in Fig. 1, sulfuric acid is the only available acid for industrial application. Although the other inorganic acids are also explored in the industry recycling processes, they are not widely used due to the high treatment cost, severe equipment corrosion, and the emission of waste gas (e.g., Cl ) and waste water. For organic acids, their low S / L ratio is one of the drawbacks for further implementation into industry which will highly increase the emission of waste water and the cost.\nSince Co^3+ in LiCoO2 needs to be converted to C0 ^2+, reductants are necessary for almost all acid leaching processes, except for acids with reducibility, such as HCl and ascorbic acid. Among the most used reductants (e.g., H2O2 (Zou et al., 2013), glucose (Chen et al., 2016), Na2S2O3 (Zhang et al., 2015) and NaHSO3 ( (Pagnanelli et al., 2014)), H2O2 attends 80% of the leaching process as reductant because it will not introduce any anion or cation into the solution. The main concentration of H2O2 is 1–6 vol% in leaching processes.",

Effect ofacid species on leaching processes (both the efficiency and selectivity)\nConsidering 12 kinds of acids, the effects of acid species on the recovery rates and leaching speeds were systematically investigated. For the inorganic or organic acid leaching processes, there are no obvious change of leaching speeds with the increase of solution pH, indicating that the addition of reductant makes the leaching speed high enough to ensure effective leaching. Compared with the leaching processes without reductants, the leaching speed of ascorbic acid (acid G) decreases in the leaching with H O. Redox reaction between hydrogen peroxide and ascorbic acid is observed that the reducibility of the leachant is subsequently reduced. The oxidative degradation of ascorbic acid by hydrogen peroxide has been deeply studied in the early researches (C.Deutsch, 1998; Udenfriend et al., 1954).\nSimilar to the leaching processes without reductants, the leaching processes with inorganic acids do not have selectivity, as summarized in Table 5. The leachant with organic acids can selectively leach Co and Li while the recovery rate of Al is lower than 12 wt%. Except the recovery rates of cobalt in tartaric acid and ascorbic acid leaching processes, the recovery rates of cobalt and lithium in each acid leaching process are higher than 99 wt%, proving that the addition of reductant can completely leaching cobalt and lithium. Since H2O2 reacts with ascorbic acid, the recovery rate of cobalt in the ascorbic acid leaching process is lower than the recovery rate in other acid leaching processes. In the tartaric acid leaching process, the lower recovery rate of Co was caused by the precipitation of cobalt, which is similar to the formic acid and/or oxalate leaching process (Gao et al., 2017; Zeng et al., 2015b). The morphology of the pink precipitation was observed by a mineral liberation analyzer (Figs. S3 and S4).",

          "text": "## 3.6. Waste management of spent lithium-ion batteries\nSpent LIBs are a significant waste stream which requires adequate management (Bahaloo-Horeh and Mousavi, 2017). The management of spent LIBs has been debated around the world, including international organizations, governments, academic, industry and non-governmental organizations.\nSince it is both a local and global issue, several studies has been focused on the management of spent LIBs using the managerial tools such as life cycle assessment (LCA) (Liang et al., 2017), material flow analysis (MFA) (Sommer et al., 2015) and extended producer responsibility (RPR) (Bertuol et al., 2016). Zackrisson et al. (Zackrisson et al., 2010) optimize the design of lithium-ion batteries using LCA methods for plug-in hybrid electric vehicles. Speirs et al. (Speirs et al., 2014) evaluated the future of lithium availability for electric vehicle batteries under the MFA method.\nThe life of LIBs, similar as electronic equipment, contains product life cycle (selling, storage at home, use, reuse, giving, export) and product end-of-life (recycling, landfilling, incineration) (Tanskanen, 2013). Recovery of the valuable metals is the preferred rout for the waste LIBs where landfilling and incineration should be avoided as far as possible for a sustainable environment and society. Strict global regulations have been developed on management of spent LIBs. For example, Japan Portable Rechargeable Battery Recycling Centre (JBRC) requires the relevant producers to collect and recycle rechargeable batteries (Terazono et al., 2015). The US Environmental Protection Agency considers all spent batteries as hazardous waste (Zand and Abduli, 2008). EU legislation (Directive 2006/66/EC) restrict that at least of 50% of the average weight of spent batteries should be recycled into materials for their primary application or for other applications besides energy recovery battery by 2011 (Dewulf et al., 2010). Similar legislation for spent LIBs of e-waste is either in force at different stages in Canada, China, South Africa, Mexico and so on.\nAfter collection of the spent LIBs, the recycling processes should be carried out to recover the valuable metals. The recycling method mainly include hydrometallurgy, pyrometallurgy and biometallurgy which have been used in industrial technologies throughout the world (Lv et al., 2018). In LithoRec process, which combines similar mechanical and hydrometallurgical methods, is very useful and effective for the mixed recovered spent LIBs (Kwade and Diekmann, 2018). In Umicore process, the spent batteries are smelted with flux to form a metal phase containing most of the Co. Ni and partial Fe to be refined and a slag phase containing Li and small amount of other metals to be further recovered (Gao et al., 2017; Marinos, 2014).\nAll in all, the management of spent LIBs need enhancing producer responsibility, increasing publicity, raising of public awareness, developing green public transport, and improving the inspection of the recycling companies (Bahaloo-Horeh and Mousavi, 2017; Sun et al., 2017). The researchers, governments, producers, recyclers and publics should have the responsibility for the management of spent LIBs.",
